title: Patacara the teacher
hookLine: the woman who lost everything becomes a teacher of other grieving women

lines: AN ARROW NO ONE CAN SEE.
cards: An arrow, lodged where nobody can see it. That's how grieving mothers, in the verses of the elder nuns, speak of their sorrow for their children. And they name the woman who drew it out: Patacara.
Tradition tells her losses first: a husband, children, parents, all gone, it says, in a stretch of days so terrible that she wandered out of her mind with grief, until she reached the Buddha.
That's usually where the telling stops. Today it keeps going. The woman who lost everything becomes the one other grieving women come looking for.

teach.h: WATER DOWN A SLOPE, A LAMP GOES OUT.
teach.b: First, her own waking. In her verses in the Therigatha, Patacara tells how she washed her feet, watched the water run down the slope, and steadied her mind on it.
The commentary adds what she saw: some water went a little way, some further, some further still, the way lives run short and long.
That evening she took a lamp into her cell, sat on her bed, and drew down the wick with a needle. As the flame went out, her mind was freed. Second, what she says to the grieving.
In another poem, mothers remember her words. You don't know the way he came, or the way he went.
He came from somewhere unseen and went on somewhere unseen. So why weep, crying, my son? It sounds hard on paper.
In the poem it lands as the voice of someone who stood in the same place. Third, what the women say back.

She drew the arrow from their hearts, they say, the grief for their children, and they went forth as nuns. Other nuns' verses name her too: they did as Patacara taught, washed their feet, went to their cells, and woke.

In the list of foremost disciples, Patacara is named first among the nuns who know the discipline, the community's rules. The woman who once wandered wild with grief became the keeper of order. Grief didn't vanish.
It became a way to recognize someone else's.

how: Patacara's verses and the verses of the women she taught are read in the Therigatha, and in Theravada communities her story is told as a teaching on grief and on how short and uncertain life is.

o: a vow taken by a grieving mother
an arrow or dart lodged in the heart
a lamp's wick drawn down at night

games.q: Patacara the teacher: tap the pairs.
p: lives that run short and long
the moment her mind was freed
asked where her son came and went

s: Patacara's story ends when she meets the Buddha
she becomes a nun, wakes as a lamp goes out, and teaches other grieving women.
the Buddha's list names her foremost in the discipline
first among the nuns who know the community's rules.
she comforted grieving mothers by promising their children would come back
she asked where the child had come from and gone to, and the women said she drew out the arrow.

games.q: you're Patacara. a mother comes to you crying for her dead son. you've lost children too. what do you say?
o: tell her the pain will pass soon.
ask her: you don't know the way he came or went, so why cry 'my son'?
tell her to go home and rest.
games.why: in the verses, she asks where the son came from and went, and the grieving women say she drew the arrow from their hearts.

practice: Think of someone who is grieving now, a loss this year or an old one that still sits close. Patacara didn't lead with answers; she sat with people first, so just keep this person company in your mind, with nothing to fix.
Then let them rest there, and come back to your breath.

wordCard.voice: Salla, a dart or arrow. What grieving women say Patacara drew out of their hearts, the grief for their children. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali salla, a dart or arrow: the grieving women say Patacara drew it out.

carryVoice: Your line: from grief to teacher. The one who lost everything became the one people came looking for. Until tomorrow.
